z-m-03-01.title: A long, thin paper and a plump paper: which one is larger in area?
z-m-03-01.topic: Comparing area (laying one on top of the other, and comparing with squares of the same size)
z-m-03-01.goal: Compare the area of two papers that look different in shape by eyeballing, laying one over the other, and comparing with squares of the same size, fixing your judgment as you go, and say that another method is needed when laying them over each other does not decide it.
z-m-03-01.material: There are two rectangular papers, '가' and '나', made of thick paper. '가' is a rectangle that is long from side to side, and '나' is a rectangle that is less long and plumper than '가'. You want to find out which one is larger in area (the size of the surface the paper takes up). You have not measured the lengths yet.
z-m-03-01.thinking.0: Checking a judgment made by eyeballing
z-m-03-01.thinking.1: Changing how sure you are as new information comes in
z-m-03-01.prereq.0: Knowing 'wide/narrow' and comparing two things by laying one over the other (Grade 1 level)
z-m-03-01.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you think about which one is larger in area.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, say one thing about 'what is the same and what is different' in what you newly learned.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine actually cutting out the two papers and laying one over the other, and trace with your finger which parts stick out.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.info: The two papers are placed apart on the desk and you look only with your eyes. '가' looks long and '나' looks plump.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which one do you think is larger in area right now?
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.after: It is hard to decide just from how it looks to the eye. You need a method such as laying them over each other or comparing with pieces of the same size.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 가 is larger. The width is longer, so the long one is bigger.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You looked at the length in only one direction. For area you need to think about the width and the height together.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: You cannot tell just by looking. You have to lay them over each other or measure.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You first thought of a way to check. It is a good habit to tell a feeling apart from a check.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 나 is larger. It is plump, so it looks fuller.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You decided by a feeling. It may be right, but you cannot know before you check.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The shapes are different, so the areas are of course different. We just do not know which one is larger.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Even if the shapes are different, the areas can be the same. There is not yet any reason to state it so firmly.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.info: You laid '가' on top of '나' with their top-left corners matched. '가' sticks out past '나' to the right, and '나' sticks out past '가' toward the bottom. Neither one fully covers the other.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.after: If one fully covers the other, you can say the covered one is smaller in area. But if each sticks out, it is hard to decide by laying them over each other alone.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 가 is larger. The part that sticks out continues long to the right.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You looked at only the length of the part that sticks out. Think also about how 나 sticks out at the bottom.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 나 is larger. The part that sticks out at the bottom looks thicker.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It may look that way, but you have not yet compared the sizes of the two parts that stick out.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The two areas are the same. The parts that stick out look about alike.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Looking alike is not a reason to say they are the same. They might be the same, but you need to check more.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: You cannot decide by laying them over each other alone. You need another method too.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You noticed that when each sticks out after laying them over each other, you cannot tell right away which is bigger.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.info: On both papers, small square cells of the same size were drawn with no gaps. '가' has 2 rows of 6 cells across, and '나' has 3 rows of 4 cells across.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: If you compare with cells, which one is larger in area?
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.after: 가 is two rows of 6 cells, 나 is three rows of 4 cells, and the cells are the same size, so both have 12 cells. So even though the shapes are different, the areas are the same. If the cells are different sizes, you cannot compare this way.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Both papers have 12 cells, the same, so the areas are the same.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You compared by how many cells there are in all when the cells are the same size. You thought about shape and area separately.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 가 is larger. There are 6 cells in a row, which is more than 4.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You looked at only one row. You also need to think about how many rows there are.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 나 is larger. There are 3 rows, which is more than 2.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You looked at only the number of rows. You also need to think about how many cells are in a row.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: If the shapes are different, you cannot compare areas by counting cells.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: If the cells are the same size, you can compare by how many cells there are in all, even if the shapes are different.
z-m-03-01.s.s1.reflect: How did your thinking change from when you first looked with your eyes, to when you laid them over each other, to when you compared with cells? To compare with cells, what must be the same about the cells?
z-m-03-01.s.s2.prompt: A friend said, "The shapes are different, so the areas are different too!" What would you like to say to your friend?
z-m-03-01.s.s2.hint.0: Look for whether there is an example in the papers you just saw that makes your friend's statement look wrong.
z-m-03-01.s.s2.hint.1: First write which numbers you can use as evidence in that example, then make a sentence.
z-m-03-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are the pieces of evidence I wrote (the number of cells, etc.) really numbers that belong to the two papers?
z-m-03-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say 'the shapes are different' and 'the areas are different' separately?
z-m-03-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you also say the condition that the cells are the same size?
z-m-03-01.s.s2.model.0: Both have 12 cells, so the areas are the same. Even if the shapes are different, the areas can be the same.
z-m-03-01.s.s2.model.1: I could not tell by laying them over each other, but when I counted with cells of the same size, both 가 and 나 are 12 cells. So the areas are the same.

z-m-03-02.title: A string hung between two nails on a wall: is its length the same too?
z-m-03-02.topic: Comparing length (a straight path and a bent path)
z-m-03-02.goal: Find the wrong line in the idea that two strings with the same start and end must be the same length, and say what else is needed to claim the lengths are the same and how to check.
z-m-03-02.material: There are two nails in a wall. Jia hung one string that does not stretch tightly between the two nails. Minho hung another string that does not stretch on the same two nails, but he hung it so it sagged down. Both strings start at the left nail and end at the right nail. Jia thought like this.
z-m-03-02.thinking.0: Finding the part skipped in the reasoning
z-m-03-02.thinking.2: Saying a way to check and the expected result
z-m-03-02.prereq.0: Knowing 'long/short' and comparing the lengths of two straight things by putting them end to end (Grade 1 level)
z-m-03-02.s.s1.hint.0: Sort each line into a fact you checked with your eyes and an idea drawn from the facts.
z-m-03-02.s.s1.hint.1: Draw and compare the shape of one string pulled tight and the shape of it sagging.
z-m-03-02.s.s1.line.0: My string is tight, and Minho's string sags down.
z-m-03-02.s.s1.line.1: Still, both strings are hung on the left nail and the right nail.
z-m-03-02.s.s1.line.2: The start and the end are in the same places, so the two strings are the same length too.
z-m-03-02.s.s1.line.3: So even if we pull Minho's string tight, it will be the same length as my string.
z-m-03-02.s.s2.r.a: Color has nothing to do with length. Look for things that are related to length.
z-m-03-02.s.s2.explain: When two strings are hung on the same two nails, if both are tight, both are the straightest path, so the lengths are the same. If even one sags, that string may be longer.
z-m-03-02.s.s3.prompt: You want to find out whether Minho's string is the same length as Jia's string. Write how you can check and what result you think will come out.
z-m-03-02.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine untying the two strings from the nails and laying them on a desk.
z-m-03-02.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine what happens to the other ends when you line up one end of each of the two strings.
z-m-03-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the method I described really show the difference in length between the two strings?
z-m-03-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the reason for your expected result to 'sagging/tight'?
z-m-03-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether the two strings might also come out the same length?
z-m-03-02.s.s3.model.0: Pull Minho's string tight and lay it next to Jia's string. I think the sagging string will be longer.
z-m-03-02.s.s3.model.1: Straighten both strings, put one end of each together, and look at where the other end is, and you can tell the lengths may be different.
z-m-03-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: The expected result is short, but it says both the method and the possibility.

z-m-03-03.title: If you cut a square paper once with a straight cut, what will the pieces look like?
z-m-03-03.topic: Dividing plane shapes (the pointed corners of pieces cut with one straight line)
z-m-03-03.goal: Work out the shapes of the two pieces you can make with one straight cut by looking at the number of pointed corners, and find and describe many possible cases yourself.
z-m-03-03.thinking.0: Finding the possible cases by changing where you cut
z-m-03-03.thinking.1: Sorting out the cases that do not work within the conditions
z-m-03-03.thinking.2: Explaining in words how you cut
z-m-03-03.prereq.0: Knowing triangle and quadrilateral shapes and pointing with a finger to a 'pointed corner' (where two straight lines meet)
z-m-03-03.s.s1.prompt: You cut the paper once with a straight cut and got two pieces. If you add up all the pointed corners of the two pieces, how does it compare with the 4 pointed corners of the original paper?
z-m-03-03.s.s1.explain: When you cut the paper, pointed corners appear on both pieces at the two ends of the cutting line. Counted together, there are always more than 4 (between 6 and 8).
z-m-03-03.s.s2.hint.0: While actually cutting paper, move the two ends of the cutting line to different places on the edges.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare how the pointed corners of the pieces differ when one end is put at a pointed corner and when it is put in the middle of an edge.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.ok.c0: The number of pointed corners is a natural number.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.fail.c0: The number of pointed corners is a counting number like 1, 2, 3.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.ok.c1: p is 3 or more and not greater than q.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the pointed corners of the two pieces is 8 or less.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.fail.c2: With one straight cut, you cannot make the pointed corners of the two pieces add up to more than 8.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.explain: The possible pairs are (3, 3), (3, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4). Joining two opposite pointed corners gives (3, 3). Joining one pointed corner to the middle of the opposite edge gives (3, 4). Joining the middle parts of two neighboring edges and cutting off a corner gives (3, 5). Joining the middle parts of two opposite edges gives (4, 4). You cannot make a pair with 2 pointed corners or with a sum of 9 or more.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the pairs you made and describe in words how you cut the paper.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: First say whether each end of the cutting line is at a pointed corner or in the middle of an edge.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Give names to the shapes of the two pieces (triangle, quadrilateral, etc.).
z-m-03-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: With the way of cutting I described, does that (p, q) really come out?
z-m-03-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Is it clear where you put the two ends?
z-m-03-03.s.s2.because.model.0: If you cut along the line joining two opposite pointed corners, you get 2 triangle pieces, and each has 3 pointed corners.
z-m-03-03.s.s2.because.model.1: If you join the middle parts of two neighboring edges and cut off one corner, the small triangle piece has 3 pointed corners and the big piece has 5.

z-m-03-04.title: Which box should the heart and star cookies go in?
z-m-03-04.topic: Sorting plane shapes (triangle, quadrilateral, circle shapes and shapes that are none of these)
z-m-03-04.goal: When you meet a shape that cannot be sorted into the three boxes, decide the sorting standard again, make your own sorting rule, and explain it with reasons.
z-m-03-04.material: A cookie shop wants to put flat cookies into boxes by shape. There are three boxes: a 'triangle box', a 'quadrilateral box', and a 'circle box'. The cookies are 2 triangle-shaped, 3 square-shaped, 4 circle-shaped, 2 heart-shaped, and 1 star-shaped. The star has 5 pointed corners and its edges are all straight lines. The heart has a curved line along the top edge and one pointed corner at the bottom.
z-m-03-04.thinking.0: Working out whether the sorting standard covers every case
z-m-03-04.thinking.1: Changing the standard or making a new one
z-m-03-04.thinking.2: Knowing that many different rules are possible
z-m-03-04.prereq.0: Knowing triangle, quadrilateral, and circle shapes (Grade 1 level)
z-m-03-04.prereq.1: Telling straight lines and curved lines apart
z-m-03-04.s.s1.prompt: Which box would be good for the star cookie?
z-m-03-04.s.s1.hint.0: Trace the edge of the star with a finger and count how many straight lines it is made of.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare a cookie in the triangle box with the star, and say one thing that is the same and one thing that is different.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.o.a: Make a new box. It does not fit any of the three boxes.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.r.a: You noticed that with the current standard there is nowhere to put it.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.o.b: The circle box. It is small and flat, so it looks like a circle.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.r.b: Size and flatness are not a standard for sorting shapes. Look at the edges.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.o.c: The triangle box. It has pointed corners, so it looks like a triangle.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.r.c: You only looked at the fact that it has pointed corners. The star has 5 pointed corners, so it is different from a triangle.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.o.d: The quadrilateral box. It has many pointed corners, so it is close to a quadrilateral.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.r.d: You only looked at the fact that it has many pointed corners. A quadrilateral has 4 straight lines.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.explain: The star is a shape surrounded by 5 straight lines, so it is not the same as a triangle, a quadrilateral, or a circle. You need to make a new box or change the standard.
z-m-03-04.s.s1.acc.0: If you widen the standard and rename the boxes, like 'shapes with pointed corners', you can put them in this way too. Then you would need to change the name 'triangle box'.
z-m-03-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose everything a good sorting rule should have.
z-m-03-04.s.s2.hint.0: Try putting the star and the heart into the first rule, and check whether there is a box for them.
z-m-03-04.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine that you and a friend each put the same cookies in boxes and whether they go to the same box.
z-m-03-04.s.s2.o.a: The box names are short, so they are easy to write and say
z-m-03-04.s.s2.r.a: Names being easy to write is convenient, but it is a different matter from whether the rule sorts well.
z-m-03-04.s.s2.o.b: Whatever cookie comes, there is at least one box for it
z-m-03-04.s.s2.r.b: You thought that every cookie must be able to be put in without leaving any out.
z-m-03-04.s.s2.o.c: The same cookie goes to the same box no matter who does it
z-m-03-04.s.s2.r.c: You thought that the rule must be one that does not sort differently for different people.
z-m-03-04.s.s2.o.d: The more boxes you make, the better
z-m-03-04.s.s2.r.d: Making many boxes does not make a rule good. If you make a separate box for each cookie, there is no point in sorting.
z-m-03-04.s.s2.explain: A good rule has a place for any cookie that comes (nothing left out) and sorts the same way no matter who does it. Whether the names are short and how many boxes there are do not decide whether a rule is good or bad.
z-m-03-04.s.s3.prompt: Decide on a sorting rule that can hold all the cookies, including the heart and the star. Write how you divide the boxes and which boxes the heart and the star go to.
z-m-03-04.s.s3.hint.0: Instead of the names 'triangle, quadrilateral, circle' in the current boxes, try sorting by the features of the cookie edges (straight lines, curved lines).
z-m-03-04.s.s3.hint.1: Put the 12 cookies one by one into your rule and check that no cookie is left out or goes in two places.
z-m-03-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The heart and the star ...
z-m-03-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: With my rule, does each of the 12 cookies go into exactly one box without any left out?
z-m-03-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say where the heart and the star go, with reasons?
z-m-03-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If another friend's rule is different from mine, did you think about whether that could be right too?
z-m-03-04.s.s3.model.0: The heart and the star are not a triangle, a quadrilateral, or a circle, so I make one more new box and put them in it separately.
z-m-03-04.s.s3.model.1: If I divide into two boxes, shapes made only of straight lines (triangle, quadrilateral, star) and shapes with curved lines (circle, heart), the star goes in the first box and the heart goes in the second box.
z-m-03-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is another good rule with the box names changed.

z-m-03-05.topic: Position and direction (left and right change depending on the direction you face)
z-m-03-05.goal: Explain when my left and right and my friend's left and right are the same and when they are opposite, giving the direction faced as the condition.
z-m-03-05.material: There is a teddy bear on the desk. I am sitting on one side of the desk, and the teddy bear is on my right-hand side. A friend is near this desk, but has not yet said where they are or which way they are facing.
z-m-03-05.thinking.0: Finding the conditions needed to judge
z-m-03-05.thinking.1: Imagining how it looks from a different seat
z-m-03-05.thinking.2: Explaining a conclusion that changes depending on the conditions
z-m-03-05.prereq.0: Knowing left and right and pointing in directions with your own body (Grade 1 level)
z-m-03-05.prereq.1: Knowing front, back, and facing each other
z-m-03-05.s.s1.prompt: Which side of my friend is the teddy bear on?
z-m-03-05.s.s1.hint.0: Put a pencil on the desk like the teddy bear, and as you sit, point to the pencil with your right hand.
z-m-03-05.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine separately the case where your friend stands in front of you and the case where they stand behind you.
z-m-03-05.s.s2.prompt: You were told something new. "My friend is sitting on the opposite side of the desk, facing me. The teddy bear is still on my right-hand side." Which side of my friend is the teddy bear on?
z-m-03-05.s.s2.hint.0: Stand facing a friend and both raise your right hands. Are the two hands on the same side?
z-m-03-05.s.s2.hint.1: When the bear is on my right, find out what is on my friend's right-hand side.
z-m-03-05.s.s2.r.a: You thought that when you face each other, my right-hand side becomes my friend's left-hand side.
z-m-03-05.s.s2.r.b: You moved my right straight over to my friend's right. What changes when you face each other?
z-m-03-05.s.s2.o.c: Directly in front of or behind my friend
z-m-03-05.s.s2.r.c: You mixed up front and back with the side. The bear is on my right-hand side, that is, to the side.
z-m-03-05.s.s2.explain: When you face each other, each other's left and right are opposite. The teddy bear on my right is on my friend's left.
z-m-03-05.s.s3.prompt: This time my friend stands right behind me, facing the same way I do. Which side of my friend is the teddy bear on? Also say how this is different from when you face each other.
z-m-03-05.s.s3.hint.0: Act it out with your body: which side is the right hand of a friend who stands behind me facing the same way?
z-m-03-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the two people's right hands are on the same side when facing each other and when facing the same way.
z-m-03-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: It is on the right ...
z-m-03-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say that my answer is because of the condition 'the direction my friend faces'?
z-m-03-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the case of facing each other and the case of facing the same way?
z-m-03-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think of cases where you would have to answer differently depending on where my friend is standing?
z-m-03-05.s.s3.model.0: It is on the right. My friend is facing the same way I am, so my right and my friend's right are the same.
z-m-03-05.s.s3.model.1: I think it is on my friend's right too. When you face each other it becomes opposite, but when you look the same way it does not become opposite.

z-m-03-06.topic: Stacked shapes (thinking about the parts you cannot see)
z-m-03-06.thinking.1: Making many solutions within the conditions
z-m-03-06.thinking.2: Explaining why the shape does not change
z-m-03-06.prereq.0: Counting and adding numbers up to 10
z-m-03-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In the way I chose, are all three spaces of the back row at or below the front row?
z-m-03-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you give the reason 'they are hidden so you cannot see them'?

z-m-03-07.title: If we only put the sticks side by side two at a time, can we know the lengths of the other two?
z-m-03-07.topic: Comparing lengths indirectly (chaining results from comparing two at a time)
z-m-03-07.goal: Tell apart the cases where chaining results from comparing two at a time lets you say the lengths of two sticks you did not put side by side, from the cases where it does not, and make yourself the many possibilities in the cases that cannot be decided.
z-m-03-07.material: There are red, blue, and yellow sticks. All are straight and do not stretch. You cannot put all three sticks side by side at once, and you can only put two side by side at a time. We say the length of a stick in 'number of steps'. In the steps below, you will be told the results of putting two side by side.
z-m-03-07.thinking.1: Sorting out the cases where the information is not enough
z-m-03-07.thinking.2: Making and showing all the possible cases
z-m-03-07.prereq.0: Putting two sticks side by side and saying which is longer (Grade 1 level)
z-m-03-07.prereq.1: Saying the length of a stick in 'number of steps'
z-m-03-07.s.s1.prompt: When two were put side by side, it is said that 'red is longer than blue, and blue is longer than yellow'. Red and yellow have not been put side by side yet. Which one is longer?
z-m-03-07.s.s1.hint.0: Put the blue stick in the middle and draw the results of comparing red and yellow each with blue.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.hint.1: Suppose blue is 5 steps, and write the numbers that red and yellow could each be.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.o.a: Yellow is longer. Its name came last, so it is longer.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.r.a: You mixed up the order things were said with length. Chain together the two results you were told.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.o.b: Red is longer. You can chain through blue in the middle.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.r.b: You chained the two comparisons together.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.o.c: The two sticks are the same length. Because blue is between them.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.r.c: Having a stick in the middle does not make the other two the same.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.o.d: You can never know unless you put them side by side yourself.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.r.d: Seeing it directly is the surest, but there are cases where you can know by chaining the two results you already found.
z-m-03-07.s.s1.explain: If red is longer than blue and blue is longer than yellow, then red is longer than blue and blue is longer than yellow, so red is longer than yellow. It is a case where the middle stick works as a bridge.
z-m-03-07.s.s2.prompt: This time the results are different. It is said that 'red is longer than blue, and yellow is also longer than blue'. Red and yellow were not put side by side. Which one is longer?
z-m-03-07.s.s2.hint.0: Set blue as 5 steps and give red and yellow any numbers of 6 steps or more.
z-m-03-07.s.s2.hint.1: Change the numbers you give red and yellow and check whether you get all the cases where each one is longer.
z-m-03-07.s.s2.o.a: Red is longer. Its name came first, so it is longer.
z-m-03-07.s.s2.r.a: You mixed up the order things were said with length. In the results you were told, was there anything that compared red and yellow directly?
z-m-03-07.s.s2.o.b: Yellow is longer. Its name came last, so it is longer.
z-m-03-07.s.s2.r.b: You mixed up the order things were said with length. In the results you were told, was there anything that compared red and yellow directly?
z-m-03-07.s.s2.o.c: They are the same length. Because both are longer than blue.
z-m-03-07.s.s2.r.c: Both being longer than blue does not mean the two are the same. They could be different lengths.
z-m-03-07.s.s2.o.d: We cannot decide. Either one could be longer and still be right.
z-m-03-07.s.s2.r.d: You noticed that the given information does not decide it.
z-m-03-07.s.s2.explain: If you only know that both are longer than blue, red and yellow could have either one longer or be the same. You need to put the two side by side, or have other information.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.prompt: Keeping the result 'red is longer than blue, and yellow is also longer than blue', make 3 different sets of stick lengths in which it differs which of red and yellow is longer (or whether they are the same). The lengths are natural numbers (number of steps) from 1 to 30.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.hint.0: First decide one length for the blue stick. Red and yellow must be decided to be longer than that.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.hint.1: Make one example where red is longer than yellow, then change the two sticks' numbers to make the opposite example.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.hint.2: Count being the same length as one case too. For the third example, set red and yellow to the same number.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.var.r: Length of the red stick (number of steps)
z-m-03-07.s.s3.var.b: Length of the blue stick (number of steps)
z-m-03-07.s.s3.var.y: Length of the yellow stick (number of steps)
z-m-03-07.s.s3.ok.c0: All three lengths are natural numbers from 1 to 30.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.fail.c0: Write the lengths as natural numbers (number of steps) from 1 to 30.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.fail.c1: Red must be longer than blue.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.ok.c2: Yellow is also longer than blue.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.fail.c2: Yellow must also be longer than blue.
z-m-03-07.s.s3.explain: For example, if (red, blue, yellow) is (10, 5, 8), red is longer; if it is (8, 5, 10), yellow is longer; and if it is (7, 5, 7), they are the same. In all three cases, both sticks are longer than blue, as the result says. So this result alone cannot compare red and yellow.

z-m-03-08.title: If the shape seen from above is a circle, what kind of object could it be?
z-m-03-08.topic: Solid shapes (seeing box, round-column, and ball shapes differently depending on the direction you look)
z-m-03-08.goal: Work out whether a shape seen from one direction alone can decide the object, narrow down your judgment as you learn the shapes seen from other directions, and predict the shape when it is laid on its side.
z-m-03-08.material: There is an object on the desk, and a screen hides part of it so only some can be seen. This object is one of these: a box shape (made of square faces), a round-column shape (round and flat on the top and bottom like a tin can), or a ball shape. It is placed upright on the floor.
z-m-03-08.thinking.0: Thinking of every case that is possible with one piece of information
z-m-03-08.thinking.1: Reducing the possible cases with new information
z-m-03-08.thinking.2: Predicting the shape that changes when the direction you look from changes
z-m-03-08.prereq.0: Knowing box shapes, round-column shapes (tin cans), and ball shapes (Grade 1 level)
z-m-03-08.s.s1.prompt: The directions you can look from increase one at a time. Each time, choose what you think the object is.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine looking down at each of the three objects from above and say how each one looks.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.hint.1: If you have a real can or ball, look at it from above and from the side and find what is the same and what is different.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.info: Looking down from above, it looks like a circle shape.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think the object could be?
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.after: A box looks like a square when seen from above, and a round column and a ball look like a circle when seen from above. So with this information alone, it is hard to decide between a round column and a ball.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is a box shape. Objects on a desk are often boxes.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You did not check how something that looks round from above fits a box. How does a box look from above?
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is a ball shape. Because it looks like a circle.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You did not check whether the objects that look like a circle are only one. How do the other objects look?
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is a round column or a ball. It does not seem to be a box.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought of all the cases that look like a circle.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.o.d: All three are possible. Any object looks round from above.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: A box looks like a square from above. It is not the case that all three objects are possible.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.info: From the side it looks like a square shape, and the top and bottom are flat.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now what do you think the object could be?
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.after: An object that looks like a circle from above and a square from the side is a round column. A ball looks like a circle from the side too, and a box looks like a square from above.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is a round column. From above it looks like a circle, and from the side it looks like a square.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You matched the shapes from the two directions together.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is a ball shape. It was a circle from above, so it will be the same from the side.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: A ball looks like a circle from any direction. Check whether it fits the shape seen from the side.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is a box shape. Because it looks like a square from the side.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You looked at only the side shape. Think also about the fact that it was a circle from above.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is a circle from above and a square from the side, so we cannot decide the object.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You did not work out whether both shapes fit one object. What kind of object has both shapes?
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.info: This object was laid on its side and propped so it does not roll.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: If you look down from above at the object laid on its side, how will it look?
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.after: When it is laid down, its side faces up. The square shape you saw from the side when it was standing is now seen from above. Even the same object looks different from above depending on how it is placed.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It looks like a circle. From above it is always a circle.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You carried over what was a circle from above when it was first standing. When it is laid down, the face pointing up is different.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It looks like two circles overlapping. Because there are two faces, top and bottom.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Even though there are two faces, top and bottom, when it is laid down, the one pointing up is the side.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It looks like a triangle. When it is laid down, pointed corners appear.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Even if you lay the column down, no pointed corners appear. Think of the shape you saw from the side.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It looks like a long rectangle. When it is laid down, the side faces up.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You thought that the shape seen from the side at first becomes the shape seen from above when it is laid down.
z-m-03-08.s.s1.reflect: How did your thinking change between when you knew only the shape seen from above and when you also knew the shape seen from the side? To narrow down the possible objects, what more information was needed?
z-m-03-08.s.s2.prompt: A friend said, "It looked like a circle from above, so it's a ball!" What more could you do to find out whether your friend is right? Also write why.
z-m-03-08.s.s2.hint.0: Think about how a round column looks from above too.
z-m-03-08.s.s2.hint.1: Look for whether there is a direction in which a ball and a round column look different.
z-m-03-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: With the method I described, can a ball and a round column really be told apart?
z-m-03-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that there is another object that looks the same from above?
z-m-03-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about the case where your friend might be right?
z-m-03-08.s.s2.model.0: You have to look from the side too. A round column also looks like a circle from above, so it might not be a ball.
z-m-03-08.s.s2.model.1: You can turn the object and look from another side. A can shape is also a circle from above, so you cannot say for sure it is a ball.
z-m-03-08.s.s2.modelNote.1: It said 'cannot say for sure' together with a reason.
